definition: The part of a recursive function that handles inputs too big to answer directly: it calls the function on one or more smaller inputs (each such self-call is a recursive call) and combines the results. Every recursive case must move closer to a base case.
example: In digit_sum(n), the recursive case returns n % 10 + digit_sum(n // 10), one digit shorter each time.

definition: A quantity that strictly decreases on every recursive call and cannot decrease forever, such as a non-negative integer argument or the length of a list. If one exists, the recursion is guaranteed to stop.
example: For fact(n) with n ≥ 0, n itself is the progress measure: it drops by 1 per call and cannot go below 0.

definition: The habit of trusting that a recursive call on a smaller input returns the right answer, and only checking the base case and the step that combines the result. It is the programming form of proof by induction.
example: To count tree nodes you trust count(left) and count(right) and just check that 1 + both is right.

definition: A precise statement of what a function expects as input and what it promises to return. Recursive code is only safe to reason about with the leap of faith if every call respects the contract.
example: "count(node) returns the number of nodes in the subtree rooted at node, or 0 for None."

definition: A report listing the function calls that were active (the stack frames) when an error happened, from the outermost call to the one that failed; Python calls it a traceback and prints one for every uncaught exception. Guido van Rossum cited keeping full tracebacks as a reason CPython does not eliminate tail calls.
example: A RecursionError traceback shows the same function repeated many times.

definition: Recursion in which the recursive call is a tail call: the very last thing the function does, with its result returned unchanged. A tail-recursive function can be turned mechanically into a loop.
example: return fact_acc(n - 1, acc * n) is tail-recursive; return n * fact(n - 1) is not, because the multiplication happens afterwards.

definition: Tail-call optimisation: reusing the current stack frame for a call in tail position instead of pushing a new one, so tail recursion runs in constant stack space. Scheme requires it; C compilers often do it when optimising; CPython never does.
example: With TCO, a tail-recursive factorial of 100,000 needs one frame; in CPython it raises RecursionError.

definition: An extra parameter that carries the partial result down through recursive calls, so no work is left to do after each call returns. It is the usual way to make a function tail-recursive.
example: fact_acc(4, 1) → fact_acc(3, 4) → fact_acc(2, 12) → fact_acc(1, 24) returns 24.

definition: A small dialect of the Lisp programming language whose standard requires proper tail calls, so tail-recursive loops run in constant stack space.

The GNU Compiler Collection, a widely used open-source compiler for C, C++ and other languages. Like the Clang compiler, it often turns tail calls into jumps at higher optimisation levels, but the C standard does not require this.
example: gcc -O2 typically compiles a tail-recursive C function into a loop.

definition: The Dutch programmer who created Python, first released in 1991. In 2009 he explained why Python does not do tail-call elimination.
The stack that records pending calls and where each one resumes; in most languages this is the call stack. Recursion depth is limited by how much control stack is available.
example: A recursion 1,000 calls deep holds about 1,000 frames on the control stack at its deepest point.

definition: The native call stack used by C code, including the C functions inside the CPython interpreter. Its size is fixed when the program or thread starts (the Linux kernel's default stack limit is 8 MB), so very deep native recursion can crash the process.
example: Since CPython 3.11, most Python-to-Python calls no longer use C stack per call.

definition: The return phase of recursion: frames are removed from the top of the call stack one by one as each call returns, and pending work after each call runs in that order.
example: fact(1) returns 1, then fact(2) finishes 2 × 1, then fact(3) finishes 3 × 2.

definition: A Python decorator that remembers (memoises) a function's results by argument, so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly. It removes repeated work but does not reduce recursion depth.
example: @lru_cache on naive fib makes fib(30) do 31 real computations instead of about 2.7 million calls.

definition: In Python, a slice such as xs[1:] or path[:] creates a new list holding copies of the references, which costs time and memory proportional to its length.
example: Slicing a 1,000-item list to drop one element copies 999 references.

definition: A smaller instance of the same problem, solved as part of solving the whole. Divide and conquer, backtracking and dynamic programming all work by breaking a problem into subproblems.
example: Sorting each half of a list is a subproblem of merge sort.

definition: The work a divide-and-conquer algorithm does after its recursive calls to merge the sub-answers into the answer for the whole input. Its cost largely decides the total running time.
example: Merge sort's combine step is the linear merge; quicksort's is trivial.

definition: When a recursive solution needs the same smaller subproblem many times, as naive Fibonacci does. Plain recursion then repeats work, often exponentially; memoisation or dynamic programming solves each subproblem once.
example: fib(5) computes fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times.

definition: Subproblems that share no smaller pieces, so each can be solved separately (even in parallel) without repeating work. This is the cleanest case for divide and conquer.
example: The two halves of merge sort are independent.

definition: A variant of divide and conquer that reduces a problem to just one smaller subproblem, discarding the rest, as binary search does.

Computing x^n mod m (the remainder of x to the power n divided by m) by taking the remainder after every multiplication, so the numbers never grow large. Combined with squaring it needs only about log₂n steps; it underpins RSA and Diffie–Hellman.
example: 3^13 mod 7 = 3, found with four squarings instead of computing 1,594,323.

definition: Computing x^n by squaring the result for n/2 (and multiplying by x once more when n is odd), which needs O(log n) multiplications (at most about 2 × log₂n) instead of n − 1.
example: x^1000000 takes about 20 squarings rather than 999,999 multiplications.

definition: The number you divide by when taking a remainder. x mod m is the remainder after dividing x by m, always between 0 and m − 1 for a positive m; Python writes it x % m.
example: 17 mod 7 = 3, because 17 = 2 × 7 + 3.

definition: A 1976 method for two parties to agree a shared secret key over a public channel. Each side raises a public number to a secret power modulo a large prime, so fast modular exponentiation is its core operation.

A refinement of exponentiation by squaring that processes several bits of the exponent at a time using a small table of precomputed powers, cutting the number of multiplications for large exponents. Not related to the sliding-window array technique.

CPython stores a big integer as an array of 'digits' of 30 bits each (15 on some builds), not decimal digits. Its multiplication cut-offs, such as using Karatsuba above 70 digits, are counted in these units.
example: A 2,100-bit integer is 70 internal 30-bit digits.

definition: The problem of finding the two points nearest each other among n points in the plane. Checking every pair is O(n²); the divide-and-conquer algorithm takes O(n log n) by checking only a narrow strip around the dividing line.

A proof that only a limited number of points can fit in a region if every pair must be at least some distance apart. It is why the closest-pair combine step only compares each strip point with the next 7.
example: Each δ/2 square can hold at most one point from one half, so a δ × 2δ box holds at most 8.

definition: The lower-case Greek letter δ, used in the closest-pair algorithm for the smallest distance found so far. In other formulas δ often means a small quantity.
A Python function that returns the straight-line (Euclidean) distance √(x² + y²) from its arguments, computed in floating point while avoiding overflow.
example: hypot(3, 4) returns 5.0.

definition: An algorithm that switches between methods depending on input size, typically using a fast-on-small-inputs method (such as insertion sort or schoolbook multiplication) below a threshold to avoid recursion overhead.
example: Timsort uses insertion sort on short runs; CPython uses schoolbook multiplication below about 70 internal digits.

definition: Java's framework (java.util.concurrent, from Java 7) for running recursive divide-and-conquer tasks in parallel: a task 'forks' subtasks onto worker threads and 'joins' to wait for their results.

Counting the pairs in a list that are out of order (an earlier item larger than a later one). A modified merge sort counts them in O(n log n): inversions inside each half are counted recursively and pairs across halves during the merge.
example: [3, 1, 2] has 2 inversions: (3, 1) and (3, 2).

definition: The tree of choices a backtracking search walks, often called its decision tree: each level is one decision, each edge one choice, each leaf a complete candidate. It is implicit: generated on the fly by the recursion, never built in memory. (Not the same as the decision-tree model used to prove sorting lower bounds.)
example: Subsets of [1, 2, 3] form a state-space tree with 3 levels of decisions and 8 leaves.

definition: Visiting a tree or graph by going as deep as possible along one branch before backing up to try the next. Backtracking is a depth-first traversal of its decision tree, so it holds only one root-to-node path at a time.
The backtracking template: make one choice in shared state (choose), recurse with it in place (explore), then undo it exactly (unchoose) so the next choice starts from the same state.
example: path.append(x); bt(); path.pop().

definition: Abandoning a partial solution as soon as it cannot lead to a valid (feasibility pruning) or better (bound pruning) answer, which skips the whole subtree below it. Pruning is what makes backtracking faster than brute force.
example: In combination sum, once a sorted candidate exceeds the remaining target, every later candidate is skipped.

definition: A search method for optimisation problems that prunes any branch whose best possible result (a bound) cannot beat the best complete solution found so far.
An arrangement of items in a particular order. n distinct items have n! (n factorial) permutations.
A selection of k items from n where order does not matter. There are C(n, k) = n! / (k! × (n − k)!) of them.
example: Choosing 2 of {1, 2, 3, 4} gives 6 combinations.

definition: The problem of listing every multiset of candidate numbers (each reusable) that adds up to a target. It is a standard backtracking exercise in pruning and duplicate avoidance.
example: Candidates [2, 3, 5] and target 8 give [2, 2, 2, 2], [2, 3, 3] and [3, 5].

definition: A collection like a set, but in which a value may appear more than once; order still doesn't matter.
example: {2, 2, 3} is a multiset; it is the same multiset as {2, 3, 2}.

definition: To actually build and store every result in memory, rather than producing them one at a time and discarding each after use.
example: Materialising all 2^40 subsets is infeasible; yielding them one by one needs only O(n) working memory.

definition: Regular-expression denial of service: an attack that sends input making a backtracking regex engine explore exponentially (or polynomially) many alternatives, tying up the CPU.
example: (a+)+$ against 30 a's followed by b tries over half a billion groupings.

definition: A pattern for matching text, such as a+ for 'one or more a's'. Backtracking engines (like Python's re) try alternatives one at a time, which can take exponential time on some patterns.
example: re.match(r'(a+)+$', 'aaab') fails only after trying every way to group the a's.

definition: The code that runs a regular expression against text. Backtracking engines support rich features but can be exponential; automaton-based engines such as RE2 guarantee time linear in the input.
Eventually growing faster than any linear function of the input size, for example in proportion to n log n, n² or 2^n.

The part of a package manager that picks a version of every required package so that all their version constraints hold at once. pip's resolver backtracks over candidate versions; others use SAT solvers.
A logic programming language (1972) in which a program is a set of facts and rules; running it searches for answers by depth-first backtracking.
The puzzle of placing n chess queens on an n × n board so that no two share a row, column or diagonal. The 8 × 8 board has 92 solutions; it is a classic backtracking exercise.
example: For n = 4 the two solutions are [1, 3, 0, 2] and [2, 0, 3, 1] (column per row).

definition: A diagonal running from top-right to bottom-left. All squares on one anti-diagonal share the same row + column.
example: (1, 2), (2, 1) and (3, 0) all have row + column = 3.

definition: A puzzle in which a 9 × 9 grid must be filled so every row, column and 3 × 3 box contains 1–9 exactly once. It is a textbook constraint satisfaction problem.

A problem stated as variables, each with a domain of allowed values, and constraints saying which combinations are allowed. Solvers combine backtracking with variable ordering and constraint propagation.
example: In Sudoku each empty cell is a variable with domain {1..9}.

definition: In a constraint satisfaction problem, the set of values a variable may still take. Domains shrink as constraints are propagated; an empty domain means the current branch is dead.
example: A Sudoku cell whose row, column and box already contain 1–5 has domain {6, 7, 8, 9}.

definition: A variable-ordering heuristic: branch next on the variable with the fewest values left in its domain. It exposes forced moves (one value) and dead ends (none) immediately.
example: Cells with 2 candidates are tried before cells with 4.

definition: A tie-break for variable ordering: among equally constrained variables, choose the one involved in the most constraints with unassigned variables.
A value-ordering heuristic: try first the value that rules out the fewest options for neighbouring variables, to make success without backtracking more likely.
After assigning a variable, immediately remove now-impossible values from its neighbours' domains, and backtrack at once if any domain becomes empty. It looks one step ahead.

A propagation rule for constraints between pairs of variables: keep a value only if some value in each constrained neighbour supports it, and repeat until nothing changes. AC-3 is the standard algorithm.
Deducing the consequences of choices so far, by removing impossible values and assigning forced ones, before (or instead of) guessing. Each deduction can trigger more.
example: Placing a 6 in a Sudoku cell removes 6 from its 20 peers, which may leave another cell with one candidate.

definition: A Sudoku cell that has only one possible digit left, so it can be assigned without guessing.
A digit that has only one possible cell left in a row, column or box, so it must go there even though that cell has other candidates.
An American computer scientist, co-author of Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, whose essay 'Solving Every Sudoku Puzzle' popularised constraint propagation plus search for Sudoku.
The problem of choosing rows of a 0/1 table so that every column contains exactly one 1 among the chosen rows. Sudoku and many tiling puzzles can be written as exact cover.
example: Sudoku becomes a 729-row by 324-column exact-cover table.

definition: Donald Knuth's backtracking algorithm for exact cover: pick a column with the fewest 1s, try each row covering it, remove conflicting rows and columns, recurse, and restore on return.
Knuth's technique for Algorithm X using circular doubly linked lists: a removed node keeps its own links, so putting it back takes O(1) pointer writes. Algorithm X implemented this way is called DLX.

A program that decides whether a Boolean formula (variables that are true or false, joined by and, or, not) can be made true, and finds such an assignment. Modern solvers can often handle structured problems with hundreds of thousands of variables and millions of constraints.
The Davis–Putnam–Logemann–Loveland algorithm (1962): backtracking search over Boolean variables plus unit propagation. It is the basis of modern SAT solvers.
In SAT solving, when a clause has every literal false except one unassigned literal, that literal must be made true. Repeating this is SAT's equivalent of a Sudoku naked single.
In SAT, a clause is an 'or' of literals, such as (x or not y or z); a formula is an 'and' of clauses. CDCL solvers learn new clauses from conflicts to avoid repeating mistakes.
A Boolean variable or its negation, such as x or not x.
Conflict-driven clause learning, the design of modern SAT solvers: DPLL plus learning a new clause from every conflict and backjumping past decisions that were not to blame.
Backtracking that jumps back several decisions at once, straight to the decision that caused a conflict, instead of undoing only the most recent one (chronological backtracking).
An open-source library that resolves package dependencies using SAT-solving techniques. It is used by Fedora's DNF and by conda's libmamba solver.
The package manager of Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux, which uses libsolv to resolve dependencies.
A cross-platform package and environment manager, popular for Python data science; its default solver (libmamba) uses libsolv.

Avoiding searching solutions that are mirror images or rotations of ones already found, for example by trying only the left half of the first row's columns in N-Queens and doubling the count (with separate handling of the middle column when n is odd).
example: 8-Queens has 92 solutions but only 12 distinct up to rotation and reflection.

definition: The rightmost bit that is 1 in a binary number. In two's complement, x & -x keeps only that bit.

The programming problem of deciding whether a word can be spelled by a path of horizontally or vertically adjacent grid cells, using each cell no more than once. Unlike the newspaper puzzle, whose words run in straight lines, the path may bend. Solved by depth-first backtracking from each cell; many words at once are found with a trie.
A flag on a trie node saying that the path from the root to it spells a complete word, as opposed to just a prefix of longer words.

A problem has it when some optimal solution begins with the greedy (locally best) choice, so making that choice never rules out the best answer. Together with optimal substructure, it makes a greedy algorithm correct.
A problem has optimal substructure when an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems. Both greedy algorithms and dynamic programming rely on it.
example: A shortest path from A to C through B contains a shortest path from A to B.

definition: The standard proof technique for greedy algorithms: take any optimal solution, swap the greedy choice into it, and show the result is still valid and no worse.
A proof style for greedy algorithms: show that after every step, greedy's partial solution is at least as good as any other solution's after the same number of steps, so greedy can never fall behind.
Choosing the largest number of non-overlapping intervals (such as meetings for one room). Sorting by end time and taking each compatible interval is provably optimal, in O(n log n).
The greedy rule for interval scheduling: repeatedly take the interval that finishes first among those compatible with what has been chosen. It leaves the most time for everything else.
Interval scheduling where each interval has a value and the goal is the largest total value. Greedy fails; dynamic programming over intervals sorted by end time solves it in O(n log n).

Assigning every interval to a resource (such as a room) so that no two intervals on one resource overlap, using as few resources as possible. The minimum equals the largest number of intervals overlapping at any moment.
David Huffman's 1952 greedy algorithm for an optimal prefix code: repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency trees until one remains. Common symbols get short codewords and rare ones long codewords.
example: With frequencies a 45, b 13, c 12, d 16, e 9, f 5, a gets a 1-bit code and e and f 4-bit codes.

definition: A set of codewords in which no codeword is the start of another, so an encoded bit stream can be decoded symbol by symbol without separators. Prefix codes correspond to binary trees with symbols at the leaves.
example: {0, 10, 110, 111} is a prefix code; {0, 01, 11} is not.

definition: A code that gives every symbol a codeword of the same number of bits, ⌈log₂k⌉ bits for k symbols.
example: 6 symbols need 3 bits each.

definition: A code whose codewords have different lengths, so frequent symbols can be given shorter codewords and the average length falls.
The bit pattern a code assigns to one symbol.
example: In a Huffman code, a might be 0 and f might be 1100.

definition: The table mapping symbols to codewords, which a decoder needs; in compressed formats it must usually be stored or sent along with the data. DEFLATE, for example, sends its custom Huffman codes as a list of code lengths before the compressed data.
Lossless compression that gives each symbol a code length close to the information it carries, so frequent symbols cost few bits. Huffman coding, arithmetic coding and ANS are entropy coders.
An entropy coding method that encodes a whole message as one number, so the average cost per symbol can be a fraction of a bit, beating Huffman when probabilities are skewed.
A family of entropy coding methods introduced by Jarosław Duda (first published around 2009) that combine compression close to arithmetic coding with a processing cost similar to Huffman coding.
A table-based implementation of ANS by Yann Collet, used inside Zstandard.
The lossless compression format behind gzip, PNG and ZIP (RFC 1951): LZ77-style back-references to repeated text, followed by Huffman coding.
A 1977 compression method by Lempel and Ziv that replaces repeated text with a reference (distance, length) back to an earlier copy.
Portable Network Graphics, a lossless image format that compresses pixel data with DEFLATE.
A widely used archive file format that bundles files and usually compresses each with DEFLATE.
A lossy image compression standard for photographs. Baseline JPEG compresses its quantised frequency data with Huffman coding.
A lossy audio compression format; after its perceptual model discards inaudible detail, the remaining quantised spectral data is Huffman-coded.
The header-compression format of HTTP/2 (RFC 7541). It can encode header strings with a fixed, pre-agreed Huffman code.
The 2015 version of the web's Hypertext Transfer Protocol (now RFC 9113), which sends binary frames and compresses headers with HPACK.

A mathematical structure of 'independent' sets (closed under taking subsets, with an exchange property) for which the greedy algorithm 'add the best element that keeps the set independent' always gives an optimum. Forests of a graph form a matroid.
In Dijkstra's algorithm, a vertex whose shortest distance is treated as known and never updated again. The greedy step finalises the closest unvisited vertex.
A greedy TSP heuristic: from the current city, always go to the closest unvisited one. Fast, but its tours can be far from optimal.
Finding the longest simple path in a graph. In general graphs it is NP-hard, and greedily taking the heaviest edge can walk into a dead end.
Choosing items, each with a weight and a value, to carry the most value without exceeding a weight capacity.
example: Capacity 50 with items (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120): the 0/1 optimum is 220.

definition: The knapsack variant where any fraction of an item may be taken. Filling by value per unit weight is optimal.
The knapsack variant where each item is taken whole or not at all. It is NP-hard; greedy by ratio can fail, and a pseudo-polynomial DP solves it in O(n × W) for n items and capacity W.
An item's value divided by its weight. The fractional knapsack greedy takes items in decreasing order of this ratio.
example: An item weighing 6 kg and worth 30 has 5 per kg.

definition: Making an amount from coin denominations with as few coins as possible. Largest-coin-first greedy works only for canonical coin systems; dynamic programming works for any.
A set of coin denominations for which largest-coin-first greedy always uses the fewest coins. UK coins and {1, 5, 10, 25} are canonical; {1, 3, 4} is not.
The face value of a coin or note.
example: UK coins come in 8 denominations from 1p to £2.

definition: A 1994 result by Dexter Kozen and Shmuel Zaks: if a coin system with at least three denominations is not canonical, its smallest counterexample lies between c₃ + 1 and the sum of the two largest coins (exclusive), so only those amounts need checking.

Comparing a fast algorithm with a simple, trusted brute-force one on thousands of small random inputs, to find a counterexample automatically. It is a form of differential testing; in other subjects 'stress test' usually means testing under heavy load instead.

A technique that splits a search into two halves, enumerates each (about 2^(n/2) options each instead of 2^n together) and combines them. For 0/1 knapsack (Horowitz and Sahni, 1974) this makes exact solutions practical for roughly 40 items, where 2^20 is about a million per half.
Arithmetic on exact fractions (numerator over denominator) rather than rounded floating-point numbers, so comparisons are never wrong because of rounding. Python provides it as fractions.Fraction.
example: Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 6) is exactly 1/2.

definition: The SI unit of mass. Knapsack examples often give item weights in kilograms.
If p is a prime and a is not a multiple of p, then a^(p−1) leaves remainder 1 when divided by p. It gives a quick check on modular exponentiation results.
Compression from which the original data can be recovered exactly, bit for bit. DEFLATE, PNG and Huffman coding are lossless.

Compression that discards detail judged unimportant (for example sounds you can't hear), so the original cannot be recovered exactly but files are much smaller. JPEG and MP3 are lossy; baseline JPEG and MP3 still use lossless Huffman coding as a final stage.
A tool that installs, upgrades and removes software packages along with the other packages they depend on, choosing compatible versions.
example: pip, conda and DNF are package managers.

definition: A function that wraps another function to add behaviour, applied with the @name syntax above a definition.
example: @functools.lru_cache above def fib(n): adds result caching to fib.

definition: The Python keyword that turns a function into a generator: each yield hands one value to the caller and pauses the function until the next value is requested, so results can be processed one at a time without storing them all.
example: Yielding each permutation lets you process all 12! orderings without storing them.

definition: Python's standard-library module of fast iterator building blocks, including permutations and combinations, which yield results in lexicographic order for sorted input.
A lossless compression format and library designed by Yann Collet at Facebook (RFC 8878). It combines LZ77-style matching with Huffman coding for literals and FSE, an ANS variant, for other symbols.
A widely used file compression format and tool (RFC 1952) whose compressed data is DEFLATE: LZ77-style back-references followed by Huffman coding.

An open-source compiler for C, C++ and Objective-C from the LLVM project, the main alternative to GCC. Like GCC, it often turns tail calls into jumps when optimising, but the C standard does not require it.
